explanations.explanation: I see why you went there, since Eliphaz asks whether God profits from Job's blameless ways (Job 22:3). But look at how he asks it: “Does it delight the Almighty that you are righteous?” I think he's hinting that God gains nothing from Job's goodness, not that God profits. So the answer is False.

Right. Eliphaz asks “Does He profit if your ways are blameless?” and I think the question is meant to have a no hiding in it (Job 22:3). He's saying God doesn't gain from Job's goodness. Eliphaz is a friend of Job's (Job 2:11), and he's leaning hard on that point.

Yep. Eliphaz asks, “Is not your wickedness great? Are not your iniquities endless?” (Job 22:5). That's his answer to why Job is hurting. Notice he says it as a question, which is a very polite way to swing a hammer.

Not this time. Job's children don't come up anywhere in this passage. Eliphaz aims the whole thing straight at Job: “Is not your wickedness great?” (Job 22:5). The blame never leaves Job's side of the table.

Ha, that would be a plot twist, friend. But Eliphaz never says a word about his friends' advice. He points at Job and says, “Is not your wickedness great? Are not your iniquities endless?” (Job 22:5).

That's it. Eliphaz says, “You gave no water to the weary and withheld food from the famished” (Job 22:7). Those are his words, and they're part of his list. Water for the thirsty, food for the hungry, and he says Job held both back.

explanations.answer: Charged them for water and food
explanations.explanation: Close to something a shopkeeper would do, but that's not in the verse. Eliphaz never mentions a price. He says Job “gave no water” and “withheld food” (Job 22:7). Nothing was sold, according to him.

explanations.answer: Sent them away to another town
explanations.explanation: That's a mix-up with the next card, friend. No town comes up in this verse. For the weary and the famished, Eliphaz says Job gave no water and withheld food (Job 22:7). The sending away comes later, and it's about widows.
Yes. Eliphaz says, “You sent widows away empty-handed” (Job 22:9). Widows are first on this part of the list. I think this one hits hard to hear, even as an accusation.
That's the one. Eliphaz says “the strength of the fatherless was crushed” (Job 22:9). The fatherless are children without a dad. He says it as part of his charge against Job.
Soldiers never march into this verse, friend. Eliphaz names widows and the fatherless (Job 22:9). He's talking about people with no one to stand up for them.
Merchants would at least have something to sell, but they're not in this verse. Eliphaz says Job sent widows away empty-handed (Job 22:9). Empty hands are the whole point.
No priests here, friend. Eliphaz's words in this verse are about widows and the fatherless (Job 22:9). You can fill that blank with “widows,” and the other with “fatherless.”

You got it. Eliphaz says, “it is so dark you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you” (Job 22:11). Dark and wet at the same time sounds like the worst power outage ever. He's describing Job's trouble that way.
Dust would make sense with the dark, but the verse says water. Eliphaz says “a flood of water covers you” (Job 22:11). No dust anywhere in it.
Locusts would be a whole other bad day, friend. But they're not in this verse. After the darkness, Eliphaz says “a flood of water covers you” (Job 22:11).

Correct. Eliphaz claims Job says, “Thick clouds veil Him so He does not see us as He traverses the vault of heaven” (Job 22:14). Notice that this is what Eliphaz says Job says. It comes right after he asks, “What does God know?” (Job 22:13).

It's actually True. Eliphaz puts these words in Job's mouth: “Thick clouds veil Him so He does not see us” (Job 22:14). It's Eliphaz's claim about what Job says. He also has Job asking, “What does God know?” (Job 22:13).

That's it. Eliphaz says they told God, “Depart from us. What can the Almighty do to us?” (Job 22:17). Those are the words he gives the wicked men of long ago. They sent God away, and it didn't go well for them, he says.
Nope. In Eliphaz's words, those men said, “Depart from us” (Job 22:17). Nothing about blessing in what they say. The houses come up in the next verse, and it's about what God did.
Not here, friend. Eliphaz says those men told God, “Depart from us. What can the Almighty do to us?” (Job 22:17). It's not a prayer for forgiveness, it's more like a door being shut.
Right. Eliphaz says, “But it was He who filled their houses with good things” (Job 22:18). So the good things came from God, in his telling. That's after they said, “Depart from us.”
The verse says the opposite. Eliphaz says, “But it was He who filled their houses with good things” (Job 22:18). The “He” is God. So the answer is True.
Yes. Eliphaz says, “The righteous see it and are glad” (Job 22:19). That's how he pictures the righteous reacting when the wicked are destroyed. It's his picture, and he gives it in one short line.
Not quite. Eliphaz says the righteous “see it and are glad” (Job 22:19). Afraid isn't in the verse.
They're not quiet in this verse, friend. Eliphaz says “the righteous see it and are glad,” and then the innocent speak up and mock (Job 22:19).

That's it. Eliphaz says, “Receive instruction from His mouth, and lay up His words in your heart” (Job 22:22). Not just hear them, but store them. Like keeping the good recipe where you can't lose it.
Doorposts are a fine place for a sign, but Eliphaz doesn't mention them. He says, “lay up His words in your heart” (Job 22:22). It's about what's inside.
A scroll would keep them neat, but that's not what he says. Eliphaz tells Job to “lay up His words in your heart” (Job 22:22). The heart is the storage place.
Yep. Eliphaz says, “If you return to the Almighty, you will be restored” (Job 22:23). It's a promise with an “if” in front. He goes on to talk about removing injustice from Job's tents.
It's actually True, friend. Eliphaz says, “If you return to the Almighty, you will be restored” (Job 22:23). That's the promise he makes.
Yes. Eliphaz says, “then the Almighty will be your gold and the finest silver for you” (Job 22:25). Not a thing God gives, but God Himself. That's his offer after he talks about the gold of Ophir.
Tents do show up in this passage, but not here. Eliphaz says, “If you remove injustice from your tents” (Job 22:23). The gold and silver in verse 25 are the Almighty Himself.

Good guess, since flocks are riches, but they're not in this verse. Eliphaz says, “then the Almighty will be your gold and the finest silver for you” (Job 22:25). It's God Himself who is the treasure.
It's the other way around, friend. Eliphaz says, “You will pray to Him, and He will hear you” (Job 22:27). God hears, he says. Silence isn't in that promise.
Right. Eliphaz says, “You will pray to Him, and He will hear you, and you will fulfill your vows” (Job 22:27). God hears, according to him. That's part of his picture of a comeback.
That's the one. Eliphaz says, “light will shine on your ways” (Job 22:28). Earlier he said it was so dark Job could not see (Job 22:11). Now he promises the opposite.
Fire does show up in the passage, but not here. In verse 20 it's about “fire has consumed their excess.” For Job's ways, Eliphaz says “light will shine” (Job 22:28).
Lightning would sure light things up, but it's not in the verse. Eliphaz says “light will shine on your ways” (Job 22:28). Quieter than lightning, and a lot easier on the nerves.

explanations.answer: Even one who is not innocent
explanations.explanation: Yes. Eliphaz says, “He will deliver even one who is not innocent, rescuing him through the cleanness of your hands” (Job 22:30). That's the last line he speaks in this passage. The rescue comes through Job's clean hands, he says.
The verse goes the other way, friend. Eliphaz says God “will deliver even one who is not innocent” (Job 22:30). That “even” makes all the difference.
Job's household doesn't come up in this verse. Eliphaz says God “will deliver even one who is not innocent” (Job 22:30). It's about someone who is not innocent.
